sourceTitle: How Do We Keep an Eye on Asteroids?
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original astronomy assessment variant; factual, CEFR and pedagogical review pending.

questions.q: Why do scientists investigate asteroids for more than safety reasons?
choices: They are easier to photograph than stars.
They contain information about the early solar system.
They can tell us exactly when Earth was formed.
They all follow the same path around the Sun.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph links asteroid studies with evidence about the solar system's distant past.

questions.q: What can differences in asteroid shapes tell researchers?
choices: That all asteroids are made of solid metal.
That every asteroid was once a planet.
That asteroids never change after they form.
That small space objects have developed and broken apart over time.
questions.explanation: Paragraph one says irregular shapes can reveal how these bodies formed and were broken apart.

questions.q: Why do astronomers share measurements of the same object?
choices: To increase its speed around the Sun.
To publish a single impressive photograph.
To improve the reliability of its predicted path.
To move the asteroid away from Earth.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two explains that more observations reduce uncertainty and sometimes change forecasts.

questions.q: What can we conclude about a newly discovered near-Earth asteroid?
choices: Its orbit may come close without indicating a future collision.
It will always strike Earth during the next year.
Scientists can calculate its path from one photograph.
Its exact shape and material must already be known.
questions.explanation: Near-Earth describes a region of an orbit, not a confirmed impact, as paragraph two states.

questions.q: Why is the DART experiment not proof that Earth was saved from a threat?
choices: The spacecraft did not hit the intended object.
The experiment only photographed a distant asteroid.
The target was chosen as a safe trial rather than a real danger.
The asteroid was too far from Earth to be observed.
questions.explanation: Paragraph three describes a controlled experiment on a system posing no collision threat.

questions.q: What did the change to Dimorphos demonstrate?
choices: A spacecraft can alter an object's motion under the tested conditions.
Every asteroid can be destroyed by a single spacecraft.
All future threats can be removed with no warning.
Earth's gravity controls every asteroid's orbit.
questions.explanation: DART shortened the time Dimorphos needed to orbit Didymos, demonstrating a real change.

questions.q: What made the Chelyabinsk event a reminder about observing the sky?
choices: A large crater formed in the centre of the city.
A relatively small unseen object caused damage and injuries.
The explosion was predicted several years earlier.
The rock arrived from the direction opposite the Sun.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four says the unseen rock caused a shock wave and broken glass despite its modest size.

questions.q: Why were many people injured during the Chelyabinsk incident?
choices: They were directly hit by a large asteroid.
The air temperature suddenly dropped.
They were caught inside a new crater.
The shock wave shattered windows and sent glass flying.
questions.explanation: The text attributes most injuries to glass broken by the shock wave.

questions.q: Which public message best reflects the author's final position?
choices: Every near-Earth asteroid should trigger an immediate evacuation.
A large impact is certain in the next few years.
Serious events are rare, but careful observation and preparation matter.
There is no reason to study small objects if big impacts are rare.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph combines an acknowledgement of rarity with a case for preparedness.

questions.q: How can accurate explanations help people who read asteroid headlines?
choices: They reduce needless fear while keeping real risks in perspective.
They ensure no asteroid will ever enter Earth's neighbourhood.
They replace the need for international scientific cooperation.
They allow scientists to avoid making further observations.
questions.explanation: The conclusion says clear explanations can prevent panic about ordinary close approaches.
